modules.title: Your Cooperative: Member Rights, AGMs and Reading the Accounts
modules.summary: Co-operative law gives you real rights — audited accounts, a dividend cap, and the power to call a meeting. Almost nobody uses them. Here is what you are entitled to, and how to ask for it.

lessons.title: What the Co-operative Societies Act gives you as a member
lessons.content:
# What the Co-operative Societies Act gives you as a member

Your co-operative is not a club that splits whatever is left over. It is a body created by law, and the law hands you specific rights: the audited accounts, the dividend cap, the power to call a meeting. Almost nobody in the average Zambian co-operative knows these exist. That is why this lesson starts with the law, not with the money.

## The law that governs you

Registered co-operative societies in Zambia are registered under the **Co-operative Societies Act** and its Regulations, and are kept on a register by the **Registrar of Co-operative Societies** — a public officer, assisted by a Deputy Registrar and Assistant Registrars, with a Director of Co-operative Societies providing and administering the services societies need. The Registrar's office sits with the Ministry of SMEs, which also publishes the *Revised National Cooperative Development Policy 2024*.

Two versions of the Act circulate with different section numbers, so never quote a section number at a meeting — quote the substance. What follows is the substance both versions agree on.

## Your rights, in the order they matter

| Right | What the law actually says |
|---|---|
| **The audited accounts** | Every society must, within **six months** after the end of each financial year, send every member who requests it an audited statement of receipts and expenditures and of assets and liabilities. You have to ask — but the answer is legally owed to you |
| **Inspect the balance sheet and audit report** | The committee must keep a copy of the latest annual balance sheet and the latest audit report open for inspection by any member, during office hours |
| **A cap on dividends** | A dividend on share capital **cannot exceed 6% a year**. Older Co-operative Societies Rules said 5%; use 6% as the current ceiling |
| **No dividend before an audit** | No dividend, no bonus and no part of accumulated funds may be declared or paid before the financial statements have been certified by a qualified auditor |
| **One member, one vote** | No voting by proxy. Your number of shares buys you no extra votes |
| **Your shares cannot be seized for your own debt** | A member's share or other interest in the society's capital is not liable to attachment or sale under a court order for that member's own debt |
| **A statement of your own interest** | After each AGM, every member receives a statement showing their share capital or other interest after the apportionment of the annual net surplus |
| **One-third can demand an investigation** | At least **one-third of the members** can apply to the Registrar for an inquiry into the constitution, administration, management or finances of the society, or an audit of the accounts |

## The rules that protect you from the committee

- **No one may hold more than one-fifth of the share capital**, so nobody can buy control of the society.
- **The AGM is the supreme authority.** The authority of the members as joint owners of the business and property is vested in the annual general meeting, and in any special meeting.
- **You vote on the surplus.** At the AGM, members confirm or amend the board's resolution on how the net surplus is distributed.
- **No member cap.** A society may not fix a limit to the number of its members.
- **The Registrar audits every society at least once a year.** Where total assets exceed **K200,000**, the Registrar may require the annual audit to be done by a public accountant.

## How big is the movement? The official numbers disagree

The Registrar's own figures show **9,498 registered co-operatives** with about 1,578,340 members as at 31 December 2019. The Ministry of SMEs' *Revised National Cooperative Development Policy 2024* reports **94,114 societies** and 1,869,005 members at end-2022 — a tenfold jump in three years, which is more likely a change in counting method (registered versus active; counting all societies rather than the minimum-membership convention) than real growth of that size. **So do not quote a single national number — confirm the current figure with the Registrar.** What is not in dispute: the Zambia Cooperative Federation reports **over 3 million members, about 14% of the population**, through about **13,000 active primary societies**, 72 district unions and 9 provincial unions. The minimum membership needed to register a society is **10**.

## The line to hold

A co-operative is not a pyramid scheme because the law says so, and because the law says so in writing: one member one vote, no proxies, a dividend cap, and no dividend before an audit. The most common real failure in a Zambian co-operative is not theft. It is silence — a committee that does not call an AGM, or calls one without audited accounts.

> **What to do this week**
> 1. Write to your secretary, in writing, asking for your audited statement of receipts and expenditures and assets and liabilities, and for the date of the last AGM.
> 2. Read the rights table above again and mark the ones you have actually exercised in the last two years.
> 3. Optional: count how many members your society has, so you know whether one-third is within reach if the accounts still do not appear.

> **Where to check**
> The Registrar of Co-operative Societies — the public office that keeps the register of societies and handles member requests and investigations.

lessons.title: The AGM: your agenda, your rights, your questions
lessons.content:
# The AGM: your agenda, your rights, your questions

The annual general meeting is the one meeting where the members — not the committee — hold the authority. Yet most members attend once a year, listen to a speech, vote for the same names, and leave without asking one question. Here is exactly what the meeting must cover, and what you are entitled to say when it does not.

## Before the meeting: the notice is a right, not a courtesy

- **At least 21 days' notice.** Notice of every general meeting must be sent to each member at the address in the register of members, stating the purpose, with the agenda made available to each member before the meeting wherever practicable.
- **The AGM must be convened within three months of the end of the financial year**, once the audit report has been received.
- **If the committee will not call it, the Registrar will.** Where the committee fails to convene the meeting, the Registrar convenes a special general meeting which proceeds as if the committee had convened it.
- **You can requisition a special general meeting yourself.** Committee members may be elected, suspended and removed only by a majority of members present and voting at a general meeting.

No notice? No agenda? That is the first thing to raise — and it is a legal point, not a personal complaint.

## The order of business, as fixed by law

| # | Item | What you are listening for |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Registration and call to order by the Chairman | |
| 2 | Minutes of the last AGM, approved or corrected | Correct them if they are wrong |
| 3 | Business arising out of the minutes | Follow-up on last year's promises |
| 4 | Report of the directors (managing committee) | What they did, not what they plan to do |
| 5 | Report of the Treasurer or Secretary-treasurer, **and consideration of the financial statement** | This is the accounts item |
| 6 | Reports of other committees | Credit and supervisory committees, for a credit union |
| 7 | **Report of the auditor** | No auditor's report? Say so, in the meeting |
| 8 | Adoption or other disposal of reports | |
| 9 | **Apportionment of the net surplus** | Your vote confirms or amends it |
| 10 | Amendments to by-laws | Read the change before you vote |
| 11 | **Elections** | Chairperson, vice chairperson, treasurer, committee |
| 12 | **Appointment of auditor**, where required | Subject to the Registrar's approval |
| 13 | Unfinished business | |
| 14 | New business | Anything you raised |
| 15 | Adjournment | |

The committee is elected as **chairperson, vice chairperson and treasurer, plus not less than two nor more than six members**.

## What the AGM can actually decide

This is the power, and it is wider than most members realise:

- **Adopt the accounts.** If the accounts are not adopted, the secretary must notify the Registrar of the reasons — and the Registrar's decision on the correctness of the accounts is final and conclusive.
- **Direct how the surplus is distributed or invested.**
- **Elect the committee** — and remove it.
- **Set the society's maximum borrowing powers** for the coming year, by directing the secretary to submit them to the Registrar. Ask what the limit is, and how much of it is used.
- **Appoint the auditor** for the coming year, subject to the Registrar's approval.
- **Confirm or amend** the board's proposal on the net surplus.

## The eight questions worth asking

1. What was our turnover last year, and what was the net surplus?
2. Where did the surplus go — reserves, dividend, education, patronage bonus?
3. What is the dividend per share, and is it inside the 6% cap?
4. Has the auditor's report been received, and is it unqualified?
5. What are members' savings and share capital on the balance sheet?
6. What is the maximum borrowing power for this year, and how much of it is used?
7. When was the last AGM, and was notice given 21 days in advance?
8. Who was elected, and how many members attended?

Ask for the answer to be minuted. A question that is not minuted is a question that never happened.

> **What to do this week**
> 1. Write down the date of your society's last AGM and the date of the next one, and check whether notice of the next meeting was given at least 21 days ahead.
> 2. Prepare three questions from the list above — one about the surplus, one about the accounts, one about the audit report.
> 3. Optional: ask the secretary for the AGM agenda and the last AGM minutes before the meeting.

> **Where to check**
> The Registrar of Co-operative Societies — for whether your society filed its returns, convened its AGM on time, and appointed its auditor.

lessons.title: Reading your cooperative's accounts in an afternoon
lessons.content:
# Reading your cooperative's accounts in an afternoon

You do not need an accounting qualification to read your co-operative's accounts. You need four documents, four questions and about an hour. This is the fastest way to know whether the money you saved is still there.

## Ask for these four documents

| Document | What it tells you | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|
| **Balance sheet** | What the society owns (assets) against what it owes (liabilities) on a specific date, including share capital, reserves and members' savings | Must be kept and open to member inspection |
| **Income and expenditure statement** (receipts and expenditures) | What came in and what went out over the year | Must be sent to you within six months if you ask for it |
| **Auditor's report** | Whether the auditor got all the information and explanations they needed, and whether in their opinion the balance sheet shows "a true and correct view" of the society's affairs | Made to the members |
| **Statement of your own interest** | Your share capital and other interest after the surplus was apportioned | Issued after each AGM |

Keep all four together. An income statement without a balance sheet tells you about the year; a balance sheet without an auditor's report tells you nobody checked it.

## The three returns a member gets, and why they are not the same thing

| | **Interest on a loan or deposit** | **Dividend on share capital** | **Patronage bonus** |
|---|---|---|---|
| What it is | You **lent** money to the society — a debt the society owes you | A share of the annual net surplus, because you **hold shares** | A share of the annual net surplus, because of the **business you did with** the society |
| Limit | The society may not pay a dividend if the interest it charges on loans to members exceeds 10% a year | **Not more than 6% a year** | Set by the by-laws, in proportion to your use of the society's services |
| Who decides | The society's own terms | The board proposes; the **AGM confirms or amends** | The board proposes; the **AGM confirms or amends** |

Two kinds of society get nothing at all. A community service society shall not pay a dividend or patronage bonus, and no part of its net surplus may be paid to a member or patron. And where a society's objects fall in the categories the Act allows, its by-laws may provide that no dividend and no patronage bonus is paid, with the surplus transferred to reserve for unforeseen losses or to improve services.

## The surplus waterfall, and the 12-month clock

The order is fixed. First **reserves**, then a **dividend on share capital** capped at 6%, then **educational purposes**, and the remainder as a **patronage bonus** in the manner the by-laws provide. Whatever is left must be **distributed within 12 months** of the close of the financial year.

**A dividend pays you for owning. A patronage bonus pays you for using.** In a working co-operative the patronage bonus is usually the bigger number. Ask which one your society is paying.

## Four questions to ask of any set of accounts

1. **Do members' savings and share capital appear in the liabilities?** If savings are not shown, the balance sheet is not showing you where your money is.
2. **Is there a net surplus, and what happened to it?** Reserves first, dividend capped at 6%, education, then patronage bonus — distributed within 12 months.
3. **Is there an auditor's report, and is it unqualified?** A qualified opinion, or a missing audit report, is the single biggest warning sign. Above **K200,000** in total assets the Registrar may require a public accountant.
4. **Is surplus being held back with no explanation?** Remember: no dividend, no bonus and no part of accumulated funds may be declared or paid before the financial statements have been certified by a qualified auditor.

## If the balance sheet or the audit report is missing

This is the escalation ladder, and every step of it is in the Act and the Regulations:

1. **Ask the committee in writing** for the latest annual balance sheet and audit report, and for the date of the last AGM and the next one. Keep the letter and the date.
2. **Request your audited statement in writing.** Every society must send it to every member who requests it, within six months of the financial year end.
3. **Call a special general meeting.** Members may requisition one; if the committee will not call the AGM, the Registrar shall convene a special general meeting.
4. **Apply to the Registrar for an inquiry or audit.** At least one-third of the members, a supervisory committee, a majority of the management committee, or a creditor who deposits security can all do this.
5. **Report the missing returns to the Registrar.** Every society must furnish annual returns and file an annual return, within six months after the financial year end.

> **What to do this week**
> 1. Write to the secretary asking for the latest balance sheet, the income and expenditure statement, the auditor's report, and your own statement of interest.
> 2. Using the four questions above, write down the three numbers you want to see: members' savings, the net surplus, and the dividend per share.
> 3. Optional: if no accounts arrive within six months of the financial year end, start at step 4 — find out how many members your society has.

> **Where to check**
> The Registrar of Co-operative Societies — for your society's filing history, its AGM dates, and the conduct of any inquiry into the accounts.

modules.title: Insurance and Claims: Covering a Funeral, a Hospital Bill and Your Family's Future
modules.summary: Funeral cover is the best-value cover most Zambians can buy, and also the easiest to get wrong. Learn the waiting period, the document pack, and the 6-month deadline that decides whether a claim is paid.

lessons.title: The four kinds of cover and which one you actually need
lessons.content:
# The four kinds of cover and which one you actually need

Insurance is the one product people buy only when they wish they had. It is also the cheapest product most Zambian households can buy that genuinely changes what happens in a bad month. The trick is buying the right kind of cover, and knowing what each one does not cover.

## Why so few of us have cover

Zambia's insurance penetration is **1.20% of GDP** — gross written premium of **K6,032 million in 2022** — against a global average of about 7% and an African average around 2.4%. The Bank of Zambia's *National Financial Inclusion Strategy II 2024–2028* names the barriers plainly: *"limited financial and digital literacy, awareness and access to information"* and *"cultural factors inhibiting the access and uptake of financial products such as life insurance products and funeral policy."* The gap is not that Zambians refuse insurance. It is that nobody has explained it to them.

## The four kinds of cover

| Type | What it actually pays for | Key trap |
|---|---|---|
| **Funeral policy** | A cash lump sum on death to pay for the burial; some products also deliver a coffin, tent, transport and a grocery cheque | Waiting periods of 3–6 months. Death inside that window pays nothing |
| **Life policy (term or whole life)** | A lump sum to the nominated beneficiary on death of the insured life | Premiums are paid for years; if you stop paying, the cover stops |
| **Health insurance** | Care at accredited facilities. **NHIMA** is the compulsory state scheme; private medical schemes exist for higher incomes | NHIMA has a **4-month waiting period** and does not cover everything |
| **Education or savings-linked policy** | An endowment paying school fees in instalments at primary, secondary or tertiary stage | Zambia abolished public-school fees in 2022, so this is now for **private, boarding and tertiary** fees only |

## Which one do you actually need first?

For a civil servant with a family, in this order:

1. **NHIMA — already yours.** It is not optional: all citizens and established residents aged 18 and above must register. Your employer deducts **1% of your basic salary** and adds **1%**, so **2% of basic salary** in total, and there is **no earnings ceiling**. Allowances sit outside the base.
2. **A funeral policy.** The highest-value cover you can buy, and the easiest to get wrong. No medical exam, no medical evidence, a small monthly premium, and it pays out at the exact moment a family is least able to pay.
3. **Life cover with a named beneficiary.** It sits on top of the funeral policy and does something different: it leaves your family something after the funeral is paid for.
4. **Education cover last**, and only for private, boarding or tertiary fees.

## What NHIMA does and does not do

| | Detail |
|---|---|
| Contribution | Employee 1% + employer 1%, charged on **basic salary**, no earnings ceiling |
| **Waiting period** | **4 months** after registration before a fully paid member can access services. No waiting period at 65 and above |
| Covered | Out-patient registration and consultation, in-patient care, ICU and HDU, diagnostics (X-ray, CT, MRI, ultrasound), major and minor surgery, maternity, pharmacy, physiotherapy, mental health and oncology, **dental and vision care including spectacles once every three years** |
| Dependants | **NHIMA's own FAQ says 6 beneficiaries** (spouse plus five dependants below 18). The **July 2024 Ministerial Statement** says "one plus six". **Give both, and confirm with NHIMA on 8000 before you register dependants** |
| When a dependant turns 18 | They must register as a principal and contribute separately |
| If the principal dies | Registered family members keep benefits for **4 months** |
| Exempt, but still register | Persons **65 and above**; persons declared **poor and vulnerable** by the Ministry responsible for social welfare; persons **mentally or physically disabled and unable to work** |

Use it at an NHIMA-accredited facility — more than 350 country-wide. Present your card or number at reception and the facility bills NHIMA directly, with no cash payment for covered services.

## Two warnings before you buy anything

**Premiums paid are not savings.** A policy is not a bank account. The money you pay in buys a promise that pays out on a specific event; you cannot withdraw it, and if you stop paying, you lose it. Keep your emergency money somewhere separate.

**Small cover sold through mobile money is a real entry point.** Low-premium policies bought through mobile money let a household start with almost nothing and add family members later. Before you sign anything, ask for the **Key Fact Statement** in writing — PIA has begun issuing these for prescribed policies, including funeral and life policies, and it is the most useful document you can read before signing.

> **What to do this week**
> 1. Check your payslip and confirm the NHIMA 1% employee deduction is on your **basic salary**, and write down your registration date so you know when the 4-month waiting period ends.
> 2. List the people in your household who would need a funeral paid for, and write the sum you would need for each — then compare it with what a funeral policy would actually pay.
> 3. Optional: ask any agent for the Key Fact Statement in writing before you sign.

> **Where to check**
> The Pensions and Insurance Authority (PIA) — for Key Fact Statements and the register of licensed insurers; and NHIMA on 8000 for your own dependants, waiting period and card.

lessons.title: Funeral cover: the waiting period, the document pack and the 6-month deadline
lessons.content:
# Funeral cover: the waiting period, the document pack and the 6-month deadline

A funeral policy pays a lump sum to the nominated beneficiary when an insured person dies, so the family does not have to sell assets or borrow in the middle of a bereavement. Three things decide whether that money arrives: the waiting period, the document pack and the clock. Get those three right and a funeral policy is the best-value cover most Zambians can buy.

## How a funeral policy is built

- You choose a **sum assured** — the amount paid on death — and pay a monthly premium. A larger sum assured costs more.
- **Many people sit on one policy**: main life, spouse, children, and often parents or extended family, up to a set number of lives.
- **No medical exam.** Funeral cover in Zambia is deliberately sold without medical tests or medical evidence.
- **There is a waiting period.** If the insured dies during it, the policy does not pay.
- **A claim is a document exercise**, not an automatic payment.

For scale: a widely cited range for the cost of a Zambian funeral is **K4,000 to K20,000**. That range comes from insurance-sector commentary rather than a government statistic, so treat it as an estimate — but it is why a K10,000–K50,000 funeral cover is meaningful rather than decorative.

## The waiting period is the killer

| Product | Cover | Waiting period | Other notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Zanaco Flexi Farewell** (underwritten by Prudential Life) | K20,000 – K100,000 | **6 months** for death from natural causes | Up to 18 people on one policy (main life, 1 spouse, 6 children, 10 extended family); the policy never lapses after the waiting period once premiums are paid |
| **FSG / Ideal Funeral Home group plans** (underwritten by African Life) | Group benefits — grocery cheque, coffin, undertaker, programme, mortuary, tent and chairs, grave cover, transport | **3 months**, waived for accidental death; **24 months for suicide** | Once-off joining fee of **K20** per nuclear family, **K20** per single member and **K10** per additional member. Schemes are **non-refundable** and need a minimum of 20 people |
| **FNB Family Protection Plan** (underwritten by Sanlam Life) | Lump sum on death | No benefit if the **policyholder's** death occurs within **6 months** of the cover start date | Ages 18–70; a valid bank card holder is required |
| **Stanbic Ubuntu Family Life Plan** | Not published as a cash figure | Not published | **No medical tests**; payout within 48 hours |
| **Old Mutual / Best Life funeral plans** | Cash payout | Not published | Claims dialled on **\*120\*6672**; aims to pay final-expense death benefits within 48 hours and other death claims within 15 working days |

**"Do not die in the first six months" is the single most common reason a funeral policy pays nothing.** Buy cover today and you have bought cover for the day after the waiting period ends — so start early, and keep paying. Once premiums are paid, the Zanaco plan never lapses, and the Stanbic plan is built around a 48-hour payout.

## The document pack

| Document | Note |
|---|---|
| Completed claim form | Signed by the claimant. **If the beneficiary cannot sign, a fingerprint certified by a Commissioner of Oaths at a police station is accepted** |
| Death certificate | Some insurers accept a **burial order** or a **medical certificate of cause of death** instead |
| Certified copy of the NRC or national ID of the deceased | A passport or driver's licence is accepted by some products |
| Certified copy of birth certificate | For a child who died |
| Certified copy of the claimant's ID | |
| Proof of relationship | Marriage certificate or birth certificate, if the deceased was not the policyholder |
| Police report | **Only where the death was accidental** |
| Policy document | Required for some group funeral plans |

Get certified copies, not photocopies. The difference between a claim that pays and a claim that is rejected is almost always paperwork.

## The two deadlines that decide the claim

- **The claim must be submitted within 6 months of the date of death.** The insurer reserves the right to reject a late claim.
- **All supporting documentation must be submitted within 12 months of the date of death.**

Put both dates in your phone on the day someone dies: the date of death, plus six months, plus twelve months. The difference between a family that receives the benefit and a family that does not is usually whether anyone kept track.

## If no beneficiary was nominated

The order is: **the spouse**; failing that, **the closest qualifying relative who is also an insured person**; failing that, **the deceased's estate**. Nominate a beneficiary yourself, in writing, while you are well. It removes the argument at the worst possible moment.

## The one document to demand before you sign

PIA has begun issuing **Key Fact Statements for prescribed policies, including funeral and life policies**. Ask the agent: *"Can I have the Key Fact Statement in writing before I sign?"* Then check three things: the **waiting period**, **how many people are covered on one policy**, and whether the **sum assured** matches the realistic cost of a funeral.

> **What to do this week**
> 1. Write down the waiting period on every policy your family holds, and the date cover started on each one.
> 2. Nominate a beneficiary in writing on every policy, and check that a certified copy of the policy document is in your file.
> 3. Optional: ask for the Key Fact Statement in writing before you sign any new policy.

> **Where to check**
> The Pensions and Insurance Authority (PIA) — for Key Fact Statements, the terms of prescribed funeral and life policies, and the register of licensed insurers.

lessons.title: Making a claim: what to do the day someone dies
lessons.content:
# Making a claim: what to do the day someone dies

A claim is not a phone call. It is a pack of documents against two deadlines, handled by people who are grieving. Everything below is designed to be done in the first week, by one named person, with a file.

## The first 72 hours

1. **Decide who is in charge of the paperwork.** One person, with a copy of the policy documents.
2. **Call the insurer's claims line and ask for the claim form.** Get the claim reference number and the exact document list for *your* policy, in writing. Old Mutual and Best Life claims are dialled on **\*120\*6672**; other insurers publish their own line.
3. **Do not spend money you do not have.** Until the benefit is paid, the family is still paying cash. Do not sell land, borrow from a money lender, or pay a "helper" who promises to release the money. **No legitimate insurer charges a fee to release a claim.**
4. **Get the certified documents started early** — the death certificate or burial order, the certified NRC of the deceased, a certified birth certificate for a child, and the proof of relationship. Certification takes time; this, not the insurer, is the real delay.
5. **Keep a claim file.** Every receipt, every certified copy, every SMS, the name of everyone you spoke to, and the date.

## The pack, in the order the insurer will want it

| # | Document | Practical note |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Completed, signed claim form | A fingerprint certified by a Commissioner of Oaths at a police station is accepted if the beneficiary cannot sign |
| 2 | Death certificate | Or the burial order, or a medical certificate of cause of death |
| 3 | Certified NRC of the deceased | |
| 4 | Certified birth certificate | For a child who died |
| 5 | Certified ID of the claimant | |
| 6 | Proof of relationship | Marriage or birth certificate if the deceased was not the policyholder |
| 7 | Police report | Only where the death was accidental |
| 8 | Policy document | |

**Submit the claim within 6 months of the date of death. Finish the supporting documents within 12 months.** Late claims can be rejected, and that is written into the terms.

## If the claim is refused or dragged out

1. **Complain to the insurer first**, in writing, and keep a copy. Ask for the reason in writing and the clause of the policy it relies on.
2. **Escalate to the Pensions and Insurance Authority (PIA)** if it is not resolved. PIA states it **acknowledges complaints within 3 days** and **investigates within 10 business days**.
3. **Keep your escalation record.** A written complaint, the reference number and the dates are what make an investigation move.

Do not stop at a verbal promise from an agent. The written complaint is the step that creates a record with the regulator behind it.

## What if there is no policy at all?

Then the family pays cash, which is why a funeral policy is the first cover most households should buy. Zambia's insurance penetration is still only **1.20% of GDP**, and the Bank of Zambia's *National Financial Inclusion Strategy II* names "limited financial and digital literacy" and "cultural factors inhibiting the uptake of ... funeral policy" as the barriers. Claims are also rising faster than premiums: policyholder benefits and claims expenses grew from **K1,887.8 million in Q3 2024 to K2,512.8 million by end-Q3 2025**. The money is moving — and most of it is going to families who did the paperwork properly.

> **What to do this week**
> 1. Put every policy number and claims number for your household in one place — a phone note and a paper copy with the certificates.
> 2. Nominate a beneficiary on any policy that does not have one, in writing, and give a copy to the family member who would handle a claim.
> 3. Optional: ask your insurer for the claims checklist for your specific policy, in writing, and keep it with the policy documents.

> **Where to check**
> The Pensions and Insurance Authority (PIA) — for the complaints route, its 3-day acknowledgement and 10-business-day investigation commitments, and the register of licensed insurers.

questions.prompt: Within how many months of the date of death must a funeral or life claim be submitted?
questions.explanation: Six months from the date of death. The insurer reserves the right to reject a late claim, and all supporting documentation must follow within 12 months.

options.text: Within 6 months of the date of death
Within 12 months of the date of death
Within 3 months of the date of death
There is no deadline

questions.prompt: What is the usual waiting period on a Zambian funeral policy, and what happens if the insured dies inside it?
questions.explanation: Common waiting periods are 3–6 months. Zanaco Flexi Farewell applies 6 months for death from natural causes; FSG and Ideal group plans apply 3 months, waived for accidental death but 24 months for suicide. Death inside the waiting period pays nothing at all.

options.text: 3–6 months, and nothing is paid if the death happens inside that window
There is no waiting period on funeral cover
12 months, and the benefit is paid anyway
24 hours, and cover starts immediately afterwards

questions.prompt: A funeral policy pays out automatically on death, so the family does not need to produce any documents.
questions.explanation: False. A claim is a document exercise, not an automatic payment. The signed claim form, the death certificate (or burial order or medical certificate of cause of death), the certified NRC of the deceased, the claimant's certified ID, proof of relationship, the policy document, and a police report where the death was accidental are what decide whether the money is paid.

options.text: True
False

questions.prompt: If no beneficiary was nominated on a policy, the benefit goes straight to the deceased's estate.
questions.explanation: False. The order is: the spouse; failing that, the closest qualifying relative who is also an insured person; failing that, the deceased's estate. Nominate a beneficiary yourself in writing so the argument does not happen in the worst week of the year.

options.text: True
False

questions.prompt: Who do you complain to if an insurer refuses or drags out a claim?
questions.explanation: Complain to the insurer first. If it is not resolved, escalate to the Pensions and Insurance Authority, which states that it acknowledges complaints within 3 days and investigates within 10 business days. Always complain in writing and keep the reference number.

options.text: The Pensions and Insurance Authority (PIA), after complaining to the insurer first
The Registrar of Co-operatives
Your local council
Only the police — there is no other route

questions.prompt: Which documents belong in a funeral claim pack?
questions.explanation: The pack is the claim: the signed claim form (a fingerprint certified by a Commissioner of Oaths at a police station is accepted if the beneficiary cannot sign), the death certificate or the burial order or a medical certificate of cause of death, the certified NRC of the deceased, the certified ID of the claimant, proof of relationship, the policy document — and a police report only where the death was accidental, not in every case.

options.text: A completed claim form, signed by the claimant or fingerprinted and certified by a Commissioner of Oaths
The death certificate — or the burial order or a medical certificate of cause of death
The certified NRC of the deceased, the claimant's certified ID, and proof of relationship
A police report, which is required in every case

lessons.title: Registering properly: PACRA, ZRA and what each one costs
lessons.content:
# Registering properly: PACRA, ZRA and what each one costs

Most small businesses in Zambia fail on bookkeeping and tax, not on the idea. Registration is cheap, fast and boring — and it is the part people leave undone, which is what turns a small problem into a large one.

## The first decision: a business name or a company?

| | **Business name** (sole trader or partnership) | **Private company limited by shares** |
|---|---|---|
| Law | *Registration of Business Names Act No. 16 of 2011* | *Companies Act, 2017* |
| What it is | A designation identifying an enterprise; you and your partners | A legal entity **separate from its owners** — it survives an owner leaving or dying |
| Your liability | **You are personally liable** for the business's debts | Limited to the shares you hold |
| Minimum people | 1 (the applicant must be 18+ and of sound mind) | At least 2 directors, not less than half of them resident in Zambia; a company secretary is required |
| Minimum capital | None stated | **K15,000** nominal |
| Ongoing duty | — | **Annual return to PACRA within 90 days** of the financial year end — **K200** for a private company |

**Plain rule: a business name is you. A company is a separate person.** For a shop or trading business run alongside a civil service salary, a business name is simpler and cheaper. A company is worth it when you need limited liability or want investors in.

## What PACRA costs and how long it takes

**PACRA registers businesses and intellectual property — it does not register land.** Land is registered by the Lands and Deeds Registry under the Lands and Deeds Registry Act (Cap 185).

| Service | Cost | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Name clearance — business name | **K83** on the BRRA eRegistry; PACRA's own portal publishes **K111.20** | **Two official portals publish different fee schedules — confirm at the counter on the day** |
| **Business name registration** | **K166** | BRRA eRegistry |
| Name clearance — local company | K90 (BRRA) / K120.00 (PACRA portal) | Same caution applies |
| **Local company registration** | **K1,000** walk-in, **K925** if the incorporation application is filed online | Minimum nominal capital K15,000; 2.5% of nominal capital K375; certificates and declarations make up the rest |
| How long a proposed name lasts | **30 days** to register it, or reserve it for a further 90 days | If you neither register nor reserve it, it expires and you start again |

The published processing time is quick: the name reservation process is completed within **24 hours** if the forms are correctly completed. Budget for your own time rather than the queue — a rejected form restarts the clock.

Start on the **Zambia Business Registration Portal (ZBRP)** — one registration, one PIN, one registration number across the agencies — and sign in with **eCitizen**, the government's single sign-on for public services. The **BRRA eRegistry** publishes the current fees and procedures for each service.

## What ZRA needs, and the tax you will actually pay

1. **Get a TPIN.** Taxpayers must notify the Commissioner General within **30 days of commencing business** and apply for a Taxpayer Identification Number and tax-type registration.
2. **Find your regime from your turnover, not from your profit.**

| Regime | Threshold | Rate |
|---|---|---|
| **Turnover tax** | Turnover up to **K5,000,000** a year | **0% on turnover of K30,000 or less per annum; 5% on turnover above K30,000 up to K5,000,000** (from 1 January 2026) |
| VAT | Compulsory when taxable supplies exceed **K800,000** in an accounting year; voluntary registration above K400,000 | 16% standard rate |
| Income tax | Turnover **above K5,000,000** | 30% corporate income tax on taxable profit |

**Turnover tax is charged on gross sales, not on profit.** A turnover-tax taxpayer pays 5% on turnover above the K30,000 annual exemption and **does not deduct expenses** — no stock, no transport, no rent, no wages. Say it out loud: *at K100,000 of sales you owe K3,500 in turnover tax whether you made K3,500 of profit or K30,000.* Filling two thresholds at once is normal: a business above K800,000 but not above K5,000,000 must register for **both** turnover tax and VAT.

**You do not compute the tax yourself** — ZRA assesses the 5% from the turnover figure you report, or that ZRA determines. But you still **file**: the turnover tax return is due on the **14th day of the month following the month of the transactions** (manual by the 5th, electronic by the 14th), and payment is due the same day. **If you had no sales in a month, you still file a nil return by the due date.** A nil return is still a return.

## The tax scam every trader must know

**ZRA does not send you an unsolicited bank message demanding tax payment.** Asking anyone for your banking details by SMS or WhatsApp is prohibited under **Section 308 of the Penal Code**, punishable by up to three years' imprisonment. Any demand for an "ID" fee, or for a bank transfer to "release funds", is a scam — and the CCPC has warned about false individuals masquerading as CCPC inspectors, who do not issue spot fines. Legitimate tax payment runs through the TaxOnline system against a valid tax invoice, or at a bank against a valid tax invoice number.

If such a message arrives: **do not pay, do not click the link.** Report the number on **\*707#** (ZICTA, works on Airtel, MTN and Zamtel) and complain to the **CCPC on 5678**. Keep screenshots of the message, the number and the transaction details — CCPC will not act without proof of the transaction.

> **What to do this week**
> 1. Write down the date you started trading, then apply for a TPIN and register the business name — the K166 fee and the 30-day notification rule are the cheapest insurance you will ever buy.
> 2. Work out your turnover for the last 12 months and place it on the scale: under K30,000, between K30,000 and K800,000, or above K800,000.
> 3. Optional: save three things on your phone — **\*707#**, **5678**, and your ZRA TaxOnline login.

> **Where to check**
> The Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA) — for your TPIN, the turnover tax rate and the monthly filing date; PACRA and the BRRA eRegistry — for registration fees and how long a registration takes.

lessons.title: The five records every small business keeps
lessons.content:
# The five records every small business keeps

ZRA can audit any period within the last **six years**. That single sentence is why records matter more than the idea. Five records, kept daily, take about an hour a week. Not keeping them costs far more.

## The five records

| # | Record | What it answers |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Cash book / income and expenses record** | What came in, what went out, and what is left |
| 2 | **Credit sales book (debtors)** | Who owes you, how much, and since when |
| 3 | **Stock or inventory record** | What is on hand, and what it cost |
| 4 | **Bank and mobile-money reconciliation** | Whether the money in the wallet matches the money in the books |
| 5 | **Fixed-asset register** | What the business owns: fridge, table, phone, shelves |

ZRA's own requirements in plain terms: keep **all business records pertaining to turnover** for up to **six years**; keep books of accounts for **inventory, production and sales in English**; keep sales records, invoices and receipts for six years; keep **bank statements and mobile-money statements** for six years; and keep **both** the proof of payment (PRN) and the filed return. **Payment is not a substitute for filing — you need both.**

**A bank statement alone is not enough** if you also take cash or mobile money. That is the record that catches most traders: turnover ZRA can see from your wallet, and receipts that say something else.

For a trader, the **cash book** and the **debtors book** are the two that matter most, and the stock record is the third. The other two matter when the business grows.

## The daily discipline

Three habits, none of them complicated:

1. **Record every sale and every payment on the day it happens.** Not on payday, not on Sunday. A sale you cannot produce a record for is a sale ZRA cannot see and a customer you cannot prove you supplied.
2. **Separate business money from household money.** Use a dedicated merchant wallet (MTN merchant or Airtel Money Pay) for the business and keep household spending out of it. A merchant payment into your wallet arrives whole — the mobile money transaction levy applies to person-to-person transfers, not to merchant payments — but the cash-out agent fee and any collection fee are your costs.
3. **Reconcile mobile money weekly against the statement.** Take the wallet statement, take your cash book, and make them agree. Every week. A month of drift cannot be unpicked.

## The cost of doing business, honestly

| Cost | Amount |
|---|---|
| Business name registration (PACRA) | **K166** |
| Local company registration (PACRA) | **K1,000** walk-in, **K925** online |
| Turnover tax | **5% of gross turnover above K30,000 a year**, up to K5,000,000 |
| VAT (if turnover exceeds K800,000) | 16% |
| Records to keep | 6 years |
| Late payment penalty | **Sources conflict** — one practitioner source reports **0.5% of unpaid tax per month** from 1 January 2026, while ZRA's older turnover tax leaflet states a flat **250 penalty units (K75.00) per month**. **Confirm the current figure with ZRA** |

None of those registration costs is what kills a small business. The turnover tax at 5% of gross turnover does more damage than the K166 fee ever will — and that is precisely why the cash book matters so much: **the tax is computed on the sales you recorded**, and the sales you failed to record are the ones that will be used against you.

> **What to do this week**
> 1. Start a cash book today — one page for money in, one for money out, one line per transaction, dated.
> 2. Open a separate wallet for the business and move your business money into it today.
> 3. Optional: list everyone who owes you money and how much, and start the credit sales book.

> **Where to check**
> The Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA) — for the turnover tax rate, the records you must keep, and the current late-payment penalty.

questions.prompt: Under the turnover tax rules in force from 1 January 2026, how much turnover tax does a business with turnover of K100,000 in a year owe?
questions.explanation: Turnover tax is 0% on the first K30,000 of turnover per annum and 5% on turnover above K30,000 up to K5 million, and it is charged on gross sales, not on profit. On K100,000 that is 5% of K70,000 = K3,500. No expenses are deducted.

options.text: K3,500 — 5% on the turnover above K30,000
K5,000 — 5% on the whole K100,000 of sales
30% of the profit
Nothing — turnover tax only starts above K800,000

questions.prompt: Turnover tax is charged on gross sales, so a business that is barely breaking even can still owe turnover tax.
questions.explanation: True. A turnover-tax taxpayer pays 5% on turnover above the K30,000 annual exemption and does not deduct expenses — no stock, transport, rent or wages. That is why gross sales must be recorded even in a bad month.

options.text: True
False

questions.prompt: What does PACRA register in Zambia?
questions.explanation: PACRA registers business names, companies and intellectual property — trademarks, patents, copyright, industrial designs — plus the movable-property collateral registry. It does not register land: that is the Lands and Deeds Registry under the Lands and Deeds Registry Act (Cap 185).

options.text: Companies, business names and intellectual property — but not land
Land, houses and property titles
Only companies with more than two shareholders
Mobile money merchant licences

questions.prompt: By which day of the month must a turnover tax return be filed?
questions.explanation: The return is due on the 14th day of the month following the month of the transactions — manually by the 5th, electronically by the 14th — and payment is due the same day. If you had no sales in a month, you still file a nil return by the due date.

options.text: The 14th of the month following the month of the transactions
The 5th, if you file by hand — there is no electronic filing
The end of the quarter
The last day of the same month

questions.prompt: Which of these are among the five records every small business keeps?
questions.explanation: The five are the cash book, the credit sales (debtors) book, the stock or inventory record, the bank and mobile-money reconciliation, and the fixed-asset register. You must also keep the filed ZRA return and its proof of payment for six years — those are what prove the turnover you declared. ZRA expects books of accounts for inventory, production and sales to be kept in English.

options.text: Cash book — money in and money out
Credit sales book (debtors) — who owes you and since when
Stock or inventory record
A copy of the minutes of the last general meeting
